intro: About 1.2 billion people, roughly one in seven people on Earth, are Hindus. On any given morning, many of them light a lamp at a home shrine, offer a flower to an image of Ganesha or Krishna, or chant a verse older than any other scripture still in daily use. In the Chicago area, Hindu families worship at temples in Lemont, Aurora and beyond, shop for festival sweets on Devon Avenue, and take their children to weekend classes to learn the great stories.

Hinduism is hard to fit into the categories people often use for religion. It has no single founder, no single book and no central authority. It includes worshipers of Vishnu, of Shiva and of the Goddess, philosophers who speak of one ultimate reality, and poets who sing their love for a personal God. Its texts range from the ancient Vedas and Upanishads to the epics, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, and the Bhagavad Gita, which Swami Vivekananda quoted to an American audience in Chicago in 1893.

In this unit you will read those texts and the ideas they carry: Brahman and atman, samsara and karma, dharma and moksha. You will meet the many deities and the several paths Hindus describe, visit puja and festivals, and study the history and reform of caste. Then you will sit in Arjuna's chariot, follow Krishna's answer, and see how readers from Shankara to Gandhi have understood it. By the end you should be able to explain these ideas accurately, attribute them to the traditions that hold them, and compare readings fairly.
bigQuestion: How do Hindu traditions answer the question of how to live rightly in the world while seeking freedom from it?

timeline.t: The earliest hymns of the Rig Veda are composed and passed down orally
The early Upanishads explore Brahman, atman and the self
The Mahabharata and Ramayana begin to take shape over several centuries
The Bhagavad Gita likely reaches its form, by many scholars' estimates (dates debated)
Shankara teaches Advaita, reading the Upanishads and the Gita as non-dualism
Ramanuja teaches devotion to a personal God as the heart of the Gita
Bhakti poets Mirabai and Tulsidas sing and retell the stories of Krishna and Rama
Charles Wilkins publishes the first English translation of the Gita
Swami Vivekananda speaks at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago
B. R. Ambedkar converts to Buddhism with many followers in protest against caste
The United Nations declares June 21 the International Day of Yoga

words.d: a name many Hindus use for their tradition, often translated as the eternal way or eternal order
the four oldest Hindu scriptures, hymns and ritual texts in Sanskrit, regarded as shruti
philosophical texts at the end of the Vedas about ultimate reality and the self
the one ultimate reality that underlies and pervades everything
the true, eternal self in each being
the cycle of birth, death and rebirth
action and its results, which shape one's future and future lives
duty, right conduct and moral order suited to one's role and stage of life
liberation from the cycle of rebirth
a form in which a deity, especially Vishnu, descends to earth
worship through offerings of light, flowers, food and prayer
the Gita's path of doing one's duty without selfish attachment to results

test.q: Why is Hinduism often described as a family of traditions?
choices: It was founded by one family in Ayodhya
It has no single founder, book or central authority, and its practices vary widely
It is practiced only at home
Every Hindu worships the same single deity
test.why: Hinduism has shared ideas and stories but no single founder, book or authority, so scholars call it a family of traditions.

test.q: Which texts are called shruti, what is heard?
choices: The Vedas, including the Upanishads
The Ramayana and the Mahabharata
The Puranas
The Yoga Sutras
test.why: The Vedas, with the Upanishads at their end, are shruti. The epics and Puranas are smriti.

test.q: In the Chandogya Upanishad, what does salt dissolved in water illustrate?
choices: The need to fast
The flood that destroyed the world
An unseen essence present in everything, which is also the self
The cleansing power of the Ganges
test.why: The salt cannot be seen but is tasted everywhere, like the essence that is the self of all things.

test.q: What is the relationship between karma and samsara?
choices: Karma ends samsara immediately
Samsara is a festival and karma is a prayer
They are two names for moksha
Karma, the results of actions, shapes rebirth within samsara
test.why: Karma shapes future lives within samsara, the cycle of rebirth.

test.q: Which of the four goals of life is final release from rebirth?
choices: Artha
Moksha
Kama
Dharma
test.why: Moksha is liberation. Artha is prosperity, kama is pleasure and love, and dharma is right living.

test.q: According to Gita 4.7–8, why does Vishnu take form as an avatar?
choices: To protect the good and restore dharma when it declines
To write the Vedas
To found a new religion
To punish all humans
test.why: Krishna says he comes age after age to protect the good and set dharma firmly in place.

test.q: Which pairing of deity and description is correct?
choices: Ganesha: the dancing destroyer
Shiva: the elephant-headed remover of obstacles
Lakshmi: the goddess of good fortune honored at Diwali
Vishnu: the fire god of the Rig Veda
test.why: Lakshmi is honored at Diwali. Ganesha removes obstacles, Shiva is the dancer, and Agni is the Vedic fire god.

choices: The sacred image of a deity
A lamp waved in worship
A Vedic chant
Food offered to a deity and shared with worshipers as a blessing
test.why: Prasad is blessed food, first offered to the deity in puja, then shared.

test.q: What did B. R. Ambedkar do?
choices: He wrote the Ramcharitmanas
He chaired the committee that drafted India's Constitution and fought caste discrimination
He translated the Gita into English in 1785
He founded ISKCON in New York
test.why: Ambedkar, a Dalit leader, fought caste discrimination, chaired the drafting committee and became a Buddhist in 1956.

test.q: Why does Arjuna refuse to fight at the start of the Gita?
choices: He is afraid of Krishna
He has lost his bow
He believes the war is already won
He sees his teachers and relatives in the opposing army
test.why: Arjuna sees Bhishma, Drona and his cousins across the field and cannot bring himself to kill them.

test.q: What does the Gita teach about a person's right to the fruits of action?
choices: One has a right to the work, never to its fruits
One should act only when success is certain
One should avoid all work
One has a right only to the fruits, not the work
test.why: Gita 2.47 teaches that one's right is to action alone, not its results.

test.q: Which path in the Gita and Hindu tradition centers on loving devotion to a personal God?
choices: Jnana yoga
Hatha yoga
Bhakti yoga
Karma yoga
test.why: Bhakti yoga is devotion. Jnana is knowledge, and karma yoga is selfless action.

test.q: How did Gandhi read the battle of Kurukshetra?
choices: As a model for war against the British
As an allegory of the struggle within every person between good and evil
As a story with no moral meaning
As a history of the Vedic period
test.why: Gandhi read the battle as inner struggle and drew from the Gita a teaching of selfless, nonviolent action.

test.q: What connects Swami Vivekananda to Chicago?
choices: He founded the temple in Aurora
He wrote Walden there
He translated the Ramayana there
He spoke at the World's Parliament of Religions there in 1893
test.why: Vivekananda addressed the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago.

test.q: How do the Yoga Sutras attributed to Patanjali define yoga?
choices: Stilling the movements of the mind
A set of exercises for strength
Worship of Shiva alone
The study of Sanskrit grammar
test.why: The Yoga Sutras define yoga as stilling the mind, with posture as only one of eight limbs.

write.prompt: Arjuna asks what to do when duties conflict. Using at least two texts from this unit, such as the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad on karma, Gita 2.20 on the self, Gita 2.47 on action, or Gita 18.66 on refuge, explain how Hindu readers have answered him, and how Shankara, a devotional reader and Gandhi might each stress a different part.
tips: Name each text you cite with its chapter and verse, such as Gita 2.47.
Attribute every belief: write many Hindus believe or Gandhi read, not it is true that.
Use the unit's terms, such as dharma, karma yoga, atman and bhakti, and define them briefly.
Show diversity within the tradition: compare readings rather than judging which is right.
End by explaining what the different readings share.
